blocks.content: Every object in your system answers a fundamental question:does this thing have an identity, or is it just a value? Getting this distinction right is one of the most impactful design decisions you can make. It affects equality, mutability, lifecycle, and how you model your domain.
1. The Core Distinction
Before writing a single line of code, ask yourself one question about every object in your system:
THE ONE QUESTION
"Do two instances with the same data represent the same thing or could they be different things?"

["If same data = same thing → Value Object
","If same data ≠ necessarily same thing → Entity
"]
items: If same data = same thing → Value Object
If same data ≠ necessarily same thing → Entity

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/3465c281-8999-462f-ac24-243cc40f52f8.png
This comes fromDomain-Driven Design (DDD) by Eric Evans one of the most important concepts for modelling real-world systems in code. Choosing the wrong type leads to subtle, hard-to-find bugs.
2. What is an Entity?
An entity is an object that has a unique identity that persists across time and state changes. Even if all its attributes change, it is still the same thing because it has an ID that never changes.

Think about a bank account. You can change the balance, the owner, the account type but it is still the same account. What makes it "that account" is not its current balance. It's the unique account number.

ANALOGY: A PERSON

You were born, you had a name, a height, a weight. All of those changed over the years different name (married), different weight, different address. But you are still you. Your identity is not your attributes it's something deeper: your existence as a continuous thread through time. Entities work the same way.

Lifecycle of a single order.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/ae3237d1-ac89-4b21-99a7-36d473125d86.png
When the order is first created, it receives the ID ORD-001. This ID becomes the permanent identity of that order.
As the order progresses through different stages, more information is added and its status changes:
["First, the order is created.","Then items are added to it.","Later the order is shipped.","Finally it is delivered."]
items: Then items are added to it.

blocks.content: Although the order keeps changing throughout its journey, it is still the same order. That is why every box in the diagram continues to show id = ORD-001.
The key message of the diagram is that there is a difference between an object's identity and its state.
The identity is the Order ID. It remains fixed forever.

The state is everything else about the order whether items have been added, whether it has been shipped, whether it has been delivered, and any other details. These can change many times during the order's lifetime.
The black box on the right summarizes this idea:
"ID never changes, everything else can."

In other words, the order evolves from one state to another, but the system always recognizes it as the same order because its ID remains constant. This allows every service, database record, log entry, payment record, and tracking update to refer to the same business entity throughout its entire lifecycle.
3. What is a Value Object?
A value object has no identity of its own. It is entirely defined by its attributes. Two value objects with the same attributes are completely interchangeable there is no difference between them.
Think of a ₹500 note. You don't care which specific ₹500 note you have any ₹500 note is the same as any other. The note has no identity that matters. What matters is the value it represents.

ANALOGY: A CURRENCY NOTE VS A PASSPORT

A ₹500 note is a value object swap it for any other ₹500 note and nothing changes. A passport is an entity even if two people have the same name, age, and nationality, their passports are different because each has a unique passport number. One is defined by its value; the other by its identity.

blocks.content:
How Value Objects are compared using their attribute values rather than an identity. Money A and Money B both have an amount of 100 and a currency of USD. 

When all their attributes are compared, they contain exactly the same values, so they are considered equal. For a value object like Money, there is no need to check an ID because identity does not matter. It does not matter when the objects were created, where they are stored, or whether they came from different parts of the system.

What matters is only the value they represent. Since both objects represent the same monetary value of 100 USD, they are treated as equal and interchangeable. This is different from an Entity, where identity is important. 

In a Value Object, same values mean the same object, which is why the diagram concludes: "Equal → Same Values = Same Value Object" and "No Identity Check Needed, Only Attribute Values Matter."

blocks.content: 4. Identity vs Value Equality
The most practical difference shows up in how you implement equals(). This determines what "same" means for each type.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/58647e95-6b39-4efa-a850-2b8fe40d453b.png
Entities are compared using their identity (ID), not their current data. User A and User B have different ages (30 and 31), which means some information about the user has changed over time.
However, both users have the same ID, U-001. Since the ID is the same, the system considers them to be thesame entity.
In Domain-Driven Design, an entity's attributes can change, but its identity remains constant.
That's why the diagram concludes:"Same ID = Same Entity."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/ced14630-4726-41a3-9f3e-14f0537a658d.png
Value Objects are compared. Address A and Address B have exactly the same street, city, and PIN code.

Since all their attribute values are identical, they are considered equal. Unlike entities, value objects do not have an identity (ID) that needs to be checked. The only thing that matters is the data they contain.
Therefore, because every attribute matches, both addresses represent the same value object,
which is why the diagram concludes:"Same Values = Same Value Object."
5. Value Objects in Code
A value object should be immutable, have no ID, and implement equality based on all its fields. Here's a proper Money value object:
Java 16+ record: zero boilerplate
Java records are perfect for value objects. They're immutable by default and auto-generate equals(), hashCode(), and toString() based on all fields:

Value objects are great for wrapping primitives with domain meaning. Instead ofString emailfloating around, useEmailAddress email it validates format on construction, is self-documenting, and prevents passing a phone number where an email is expected.
6. Entities in Code
An entity has an ID that is set at creation and never changes. Equality is based solely on that ID not on any other field.
NOTICE THE MIX

The User entity contains an Address value object. This is the normal pattern entities own and use value objects as their attributes. The address field is immutable (it's a value object), but the entity can replace it with a new address via moveAddress().
7. When the Same Concept Can Be Both
blocks.text: 7. When the Same Concept Can Be Both

blocks.content: This is where it gets interesting. Whether something is a value object or an entity depends on your domain not on the thing itself. The same real-world concept can be one or the other in different contexts.

ANALOGY: A SEAT ON A PLANE

For a budget airline, seat "12A" is a value any 12A is the same. For a premium airline that tracks seat history, repairs, cleaning, and assigns specific seats to passengers, seat "12A" might be an entity with its own ID and maintenance history. The seat hasn't changed the context has.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/4cd00885-8811-44dd-8a41-efd8540395f6.png
THE RULE
Ask: does your domain need to track the history or identity of this thing individually?
If yes → Entity. If you only care about its current value and two instances with the same value are interchangeable → Value Object.
8. Common Mistakes
Understanding the difference between Entities and Value Objects is simple in theory, but developers often make a few common mistakes that lead to unnecessary complexity and subtle bugs.
Mistake 1: Treating everything as an Entity
blocks.text: Mistake 1: Treating everything as an Entity

blocks.content: The most common mistake. Developers give every class a database ID, even when identity doesn't matter. This leads to unnecessary complexity IDs to manage, joins to write, IDs to pass around everywhere.
WRONG: ADDRESS DOESN'T NEED ITS OWN ID

codes.python:
class Address:
    def __init__(self, id_, street, city, pin_code):
        self.id = id_  # unnecessary -- address has no identity
        self.street = street
        self.city = city
        self.pin_code = pin_code

    def __eq__(self, other):  # equals compares by id -- wrong
        if not isinstance(other, Address):
            return False
        return self.id == other.id


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a1 = Address(1, "12 MG Rd", "Bangalore", "560001")
    a2 = Address(2, "12 MG Rd", "Bangalore", "560001")  # same fields, different id
    print(a1 == a2)  # False -- wrong! identical addresses treated as different

blocks.content: CORRECT: ADDRESS IS A VALUE OBJECT
public record Address(String street, String city, String pinCode) {}

blocks.content: Mistake 2: Using reference equality (==) for entities
blocks.text: Mistake 2: Using reference equality (==) for entities

blocks.content: In Java, == checks reference equality whether two variables point to the same object in memory. Two entity objects loaded from a database at different times will be different Java objects (== is false) but the same entity (equals() should be true).
WRONG: USING == FOR ENTITY COMPARISON
CORRECT: USE EQUALS() WHICH COMPARES BY ID
if (a.equals(b)) { ... }  // true — same ID = same entity
blocks.code: if (a.equals(b)) { ... }  // true — same ID = same entity

codes.javascript: if (a.equals(b)) { ... }  // true — same ID = same entity

blocks.content: Mistake 3: Mutable value objects
If a value object is mutable, you get subtle bugs. Two parts of the code share a reference to the same Money object. One modifies it the other sees a changed value without knowing why.
WRONG: MUTABLE VALUE OBJECT CAUSES SHARED-STATE BUG
Mistake 4: Comparing value objects with ==
Value Objects should be compared using their attribute values. Two Value Objects with identical values should be considered equal, even if they are different objects in memory.
WRONG: == ON VALUE OBJECTS
CORRECT: USE EQUALS() WHICH COMPARES BY VALUE
if (a.equals(b)) { ... }  // true — same attributes = equal

10. Summary

["The one question: \"Do two instances with the same data represent the same thing?\" Yes → Value Object. Not necessarily → Entity.","Entity = defined by identity (ID). Same ID = same entity, even if all attributes changed. Has a lifecycle, is mutable.","Value Object = defined by its attributes. Same values = same thing. No ID. Immutable. Interchangeable.","Entity equality → implement equals() based on ID only. Value object equality → implement equals()based on all fields.","Never use == to compare entities or value objects in Java always use equals().","Value objects must be immutable. \"Changing\" one means creating a new instance with the updated value.","Entities can and should contain value objects as attributes. The entity is mutable; the value objects inside it are not.","The same concept (Address, Money) can be a VO or an Entity depending on whether your domain needs to track its individual identity and history.","Use Java record for value objects immutable, equals/hashCode auto-generated from all fields, zero boilerplate.","Prefer value objects wherever you can they're simpler, safer, thread-safe, and easier to test."]
items: The one question: "Do two instances with the same data represent the same thing?" Yes → Value Object. Not necessarily → Entity.
Entity = defined by identity (ID). Same ID = same entity, even if all attributes changed. Has a lifecycle, is mutable.
Value Object = defined by its attributes. Same values = same thing. No ID. Immutable. Interchangeable.
Entity equality → implement equals() based on ID only. Value object equality → implement equals()based on all fields.
Never use == to compare entities or value objects in Java always use equals().
Value objects must be immutable. "Changing" one means creating a new instance with the updated value.
Entities can and should contain value objects as attributes. The entity is mutable; the value objects inside it are not.
The same concept (Address, Money) can be a VO or an Entity depending on whether your domain needs to track its individual identity and history.
Use Java record for value objects immutable, equals/hashCode auto-generated from all fields, zero boilerplate.
Prefer value objects wherever you can they're simpler, safer, thread-safe, and easier to test.
